passage: In the college computer lab, Rafiq had eleven tabs open for the same laptop question. One review said the battery died by evening. The next said the battery lasted all day. A forum thread called the screen dim, another called it perfect. His friend Pallavi leaned over from the next seat. "You've been reading about this for two weeks." "I know. I keep finding one more thread." He scrolled again, his stomach tight, imagining himself stuck with the wrong one. "What if I pick wrong and regret it?" Pallavi shrugged. "What do you need it for?" Rafiq opened his mouth, closed it, and opened a twelfth tab. His old laptop, hanging again on the desk at home, waited.

qa.q: How many tabs did Rafiq have open?
qa.a: Rafiq had eleven tabs open for the same laptop question.

qa.q: What is Rafiq afraid of as he scrolls with a tight stomach?
qa.a: He is afraid of regret, of picking the wrong laptop and being stuck with it, and each conflicting review makes the doubt bigger.

qa.q: What could Rafiq try instead of opening a twelfth tab?
qa.a: He could write down the two or three things he needs the laptop for and choose among the options that meet them, rather than reading more.

qa.q: How does Pallavi see Rafiq's two weeks of reading?
qa.a: Pallavi sees a friend going round in circles and asks what the laptop is for, hoping to bring him back to his own needs.

grounding: Shows a young adult reading endless reviews before a decision, ending more confused and afraid of regret.

passage:
Dear Sarika,
I'm writing because I cannot say this out loud without crying. For a month I have been trying to choose a master's course. I have thirty tabs open. One forum says the fees are not worth it; the next says it changed someone's life. Each thread makes me trust my own list less. I have read so much that I no longer know what I wanted at the start. Last night I got up at three to read one more review, and I felt worse. I think I am afraid that whichever I choose, I will regret the other. Can we talk on Sunday? I need someone to ask me simple questions. Irawati

qa.q: How many tabs does Irawati have open?
qa.a: Irawati has thirty tabs open.

qa.q: What is Irawati afraid of, and what in the letter shows it?
qa.a: Irawati is afraid that whichever course is chosen, the other one will be regretted.

qa.q: What would you suggest Irawati do before Sunday's talk?
qa.a: Irawati could stop reading new reviews and write down what mattered at the start, then bring that list to the talk with Sarika.

qa.q: How might Sarika feel on receiving this letter?
qa.a: Sarika would probably feel concerned and glad to be trusted, and would see that Irawati needs simple questions more than more information.

grounding: Shows a young adult over-researching a decision until more information only adds doubt and fear of regret.

subtype: Naming the unknowns and a default [Response]
passage: Tanuja sat on the veranda step with the offer letter for the tailoring course in town in one hand and her open BA forms in the other. Her friend Nandini, cutting the thread from a blouse, watched. "Write down what you don't know," Nandini said. Tanuja did, in the back of a copybook: "Will the fees fit? Will I get work after? Does the bus reach in time?" Then she drew a line by the ones she could find out cheaply. On Saturday she would visit the institute and speak to two past students. She wrote a date at the bottom: "Decide on the first. If nothing changes, take the course."

qa.q: What did Tanuja write at the bottom of the list?
qa.a: Tanuja wrote, "Decide on the first. If nothing changes, take the course."

qa.q: What is Tanuja probably feeling as she looks at the letter and the forms?
qa.a: She is probably uncertain but hopeful, because she is torn between two paths yet turns the doubt into a written plan.

qa.q: Why is a default useful when Tanuja sets her decision date?
qa.a: With a date and a default, she will not stay stuck, and she can revise if new facts, such as the fees or the bus, change.

qa.q: How does Nandini help Tanuja with the decision?
qa.a: Nandini does not choose for her; she only suggests writing down what is not known, which makes the choice clearer.

grounding: Shows a chooser listing unknowns, what can be learned cheaply, a decision date and a default.

subtype: Naming the unknowns and a default [Response]
passage: Priscila had three days to answer the bakery in Porto Alegre. She pushed her notebook across the table to Kaito. "Don't tell me what to do. Just check my list." It said: Not known: does the pay cover rent? Can I stand the early hours? Can be learned cheaply: ask for a trial week. Decide: Friday. Default: say yes if the trial week goes fine. Kaito nodded and said nothing. She rang the baker and booked the trial. By Wednesday she knew the hours were hard but the pay was fair, and she wrote a second line under the first: "Ask for a later start." On Friday she said yes and asked.

qa.q: How many days did Priscila have to answer the bakery?
qa.a: Priscila had three days to answer the bakery.

qa.q: How can you tell that Priscila wants to stay in charge of her own decision?
qa.a: She tells Kaito, "Don't tell me what to do. Just check my list," which shows she wants help checking but not a choice made for her.

qa.q: What did Priscila learn cheaply, and how did it change her plan?
qa.a: She booked a trial week, found the hours hard but the pay fair, and added a request for a later start.

qa.q: Why might Kaito have said nothing while reading the list?
qa.a: Kaito may have seen that the list was already sound, and wanted Priscila to feel that the decision is hers.

grounding: Shows a chooser naming unknowns, learning cheaply with a trial week, setting a decision date and default, and revising as facts arrive.

passage: Two letters lay on the steps of the temple where Sunaina sat at dusk: one from a school in the next town, one from a cooperative bank two districts away. Both wanted an answer by Monday. She did not know if the school would keep her after the first year, or if the bank posting would be lonely. Sharmila, an older colleague, had said only, "Whichever you pick, you will wonder." Sunaina's palms were damp. She wrote three reasons for the school: closer to home, teaching, room to grow. Two for the bank: pay, steadiness. She circled the school, wrote her reasons on the letter, and said it aloud once: "Even if it goes wrong, I chose it for these reasons."

qa.q: Where did Sunaina sit at dusk with the two letters?
qa.a: Sunaina sat on the steps of the temple at dusk.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling as she thought about the two offers?
qa.a: Sunaina felt anxious and weighed down by the chance of being wrong, and her damp palms show the pressure.

qa.q: How did Sunaina make her choice fair to herself?
qa.a: She wrote her reasons for each offer, chose the school, and told herself that she chose it for reasons she can stand by.

qa.q: What does Sharmila's remark suggest about how Sharmila sees big decisions?
qa.a: Sharmila sees that any choice leaves some doubt, so wondering afterwards does not mean the choice was wrong.

grounding: Shows a young professional choosing between two job offers with missing facts and judging the decision by its reasoning.

passage: Marek had one hour before the client meeting in Kraków. The client wanted a price for a roof solar system, but the roof plans were missing. Fixed price, or an hourly rate with a site visit first? He asked Elif, his supervisor, in the corridor. "What do you think?" "I think you should decide," Elif said, "and tell me why." He counted: without measurements a fixed price could lose money; an hourly start let the client stop early. His chest felt tight. He chose hourly with a survey visit and wrote three lines: what he knew, what he did not, and what would make him change his mind. In the meeting he said them out loud.

qa.q: How much time did Marek have before the client meeting?
qa.a: Marek had one hour before the client meeting.

qa.q: What is Marek worried about as he chooses between the two options?
qa.a: He is worried about choosing wrongly with facts missing, since a fixed price could lose money if the roof plans turn out difficult.

qa.q: What did Marek do to make his choice easy to revise later?
qa.a: He wrote down what he knew, what he did not know and what would change his mind, then said it aloud in the meeting.

qa.q: Why might Elif have asked Marek to explain why instead of just answering?
qa.a: Elif may want Marek to own the decision and judge it by the reasoning, not only by how it turns out.

grounding: Shows a young professional deciding fast with missing facts and giving reasons so the decision is judged by reasoning, not only outcome.

passage: Beta, I am Manjula, and at twenty-four I had two offers, one to stay in Mysuru and one in Pune. My whole family had opinions. One uncle said government jobs only. An aunt said marry first, then travel. My cousin Arnab said Pune, hands down. Each opinion came with its own fear. I sat with my tea and listened without arguing, and wrote each worry in a small notebook. Then Arnab asked, "But what do you want?" I said I wanted to see Pune. I thanked everyone at dinner and told them my answer would come by Sunday. They were quiet, but nobody argued after that.

qa.q: What two offers did Manjula have at twenty-four?
qa.a: Manjula had two offers, one to stay in Mysuru and one in Pune.

qa.q: What might Manjula have been feeling while listening to each relative?
qa.a: Manjula was probably pressured and a little anxious, but stayed courteous, listening and writing each worry down instead of arguing.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Manjula's story?
qa.a: Arnab asked what Manjula wanted, and Manjula said Pune and told the family the answer would come by Sunday.

qa.q: What might Arnab have been thinking when asking "But what do you want?"
qa.a: Arnab probably saw that the others were giving advice from their own fears and wanted Manjula's wishes to be heard.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling conflicting, confident family advice and listening respectfully without handing over the decision.

passage: The Pune offer expired at nine the next morning, and tonight the whole family had come to dinner, with a pressure cooker whistling and a broken fan clicking over the noise. Uncle told Indu to stay in Hyderabad, where it was safe. Her mother said the pay was too low. Nandini, her cousin, said take it, or she'd regret it for years. Everyone spoke at once and no one asked her a question. Indu smiled and passed the dal. "Thank you all. I hear each of you." Afterwards she took her plate to the balcony, wrote what each person feared, and then what she wanted. At eight she decided.

qa.q: When did the Pune offer expire?
qa.a: The Pune offer expired at nine the next morning.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling as everyone spoke at once and no one asked her a question?
qa.a: Indu felt crowded and unheard, but she stayed polite, smiling and passing the dal.

qa.q: What did Indu do after dinner that helped her decide?
qa.a: She went to the balcony and wrote what each person feared and then what she wanted, before deciding.

qa.q: Why might Nandini urge Indu to take the offer?
qa.a: Nandini fears Indu will regret missing the chance for years, so the advice comes from Nandini's own worry about regret.

grounding: Shows a person deciding on a move while relatives give confident, conflicting advice and listening respectfully without giving up the decision.

passage:
Dear Pranav,
This week I have two decisions, and I think they need different speeds. The first is a monthly membership at the new climbing gym. If I hate it, I can stop next month, so I signed up today. The second is the two-year agreement for the flat near your office. That one I cannot undo cheaply, so I am slowing down. Can you visit it with me on Saturday evening and tell me what you notice? I will also ask the current tenant how the water and the noise are. I will decide by Wednesday. Thank you for being the person I want to ask. Charu

qa.q: Which decision did Charu make quickly?
qa.a: Charu signed up for the monthly membership at the climbing gym that same day.

qa.q: What is Charu feeling about the flat, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Charu is careful and a little anxious about the flat, since the agreement cannot be undone cheaply and Charu slows down and seeks help.

qa.q: Why does Charu treat the two decisions at different speeds?
qa.a: The gym can be stopped next month at little cost, but the two-year agreement is hard to undo, so it deserves more care and advice.

qa.q: What might Pranav feel on being asked to visit the flat?
qa.a: Pranav would probably feel trusted and glad to help, since Charu writes "Thank you for being the person I want to ask".

grounding: Shows a wise decider acting quickly on a reversible choice and slowing down with advice on an irreversible one.

passage: My rule is one question: can I undo this cheaply? Last spring I bought a cheap study lamp in a minute, because if it was wrong I could return it. But when two universities sent offers and one deposit was non-refundable, I slowed right down. Vasudha, you asked what slowing down looked like. I made a list, asked two seniors who had joined each place, and slept on it for a night before paying. It felt slow and a little silly next to the lamp. But I would have felt worse if I had rushed something I could not take back. It is about giving each choice the care that its risk deserves. Akash

qa.q: What did Akash buy in a minute?
qa.a: Akash bought a cheap study lamp in a minute.

qa.q: How does Akash feel about having slowed down for the university choice?
qa.a: Akash felt a bit silly next to the lamp decision but was comfortable and relieved to have been careful, since the deposit could not be taken back.

qa.q: What did Akash do to slow down before paying the deposit?
qa.a: Akash made a list, asked two seniors who had joined each place and slept on it for a night.

qa.q: How might someone who rushed the deposit feel afterwards?
qa.a: They might feel regret or worry, since the non-refundable deposit cannot be taken back if the choice turns out wrong.

grounding: Shows a decider who acts fast on a cheaply reversible choice and slows down and seeks advice on a costly irreversible one.

subtype: Child frozen or crying at an accident [Actor]
passage:
Monday, circle time. Trisha ma'am held up a card. "If someone is hurt, or there is a fire, what do we do?" Yash whispered with the others, "Go to a grown-up and tell."
Wednesday, recess. Rani fell off the low slide and cried loudly. Yash stood very still, his lips trembling. Then he cried too. Then he ran across the yard to Trisha ma'am and pulled her sleeve. "Rani fell. Slide. She is crying." Ma'am hurried over with him.
Thursday, circle time. Yash said quietly, "I did not touch her. I told ma'am."

qa.q: What did Yash say when he pulled Trisha ma'am's sleeve?
qa.a: Yash said, "Rani fell. Slide. She is crying."

qa.q: What was Yash feeling as he stood still with trembling lips?
qa.a: Yash was frightened and upset, and he froze and then cried before he ran for help.

qa.q: What choice did Yash make that helped Rani?
qa.a: He ran to Trisha ma'am and told her what had happened, instead of trying to help Rani himself.

qa.q: How might Rani have felt when Trisha ma'am came hurrying over?
qa.a: Rani was probably comforted that a grown-up arrived, since Rani had fallen and was crying loudly.

grounding: Shows a young child freezing and crying at another child's fall, then running to a grown-up to tell, as the rehearsed step.

subtype: Child frozen or crying at an accident [Actor]
passage: At the temple fair the noise was so loud that Siddharth held his mother Yamini's hand tightly. Near the corn stall a flame jumped from the stove and caught the plastic sheet at the side. Siddharth stopped walking. His mouth opened but no sound came. Then he cried and pulled at his mother's sari, pointing. "Fire, Mama!" Yamini lifted him and walked quickly to the open ground by the gate, calling to the stall owner and a guard as she went. The owner put a lid on the pot and beat out the sheet, and the guard moved people back. On his mother's hip, Siddharth asked, "Is it gone?"

qa.q: Where was the fair when the flame jumped from the stove?
qa.a: It was at the temple fair, near the corn stall.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when his mouth opened but no sound came?
qa.a: Siddharth was frozen with fear, and then he cried and pulled at his mother's sari.

qa.q: What did Yamini do first, and why was it a good step?
qa.a: She lifted Siddharth and walked him to the open ground by the gate, which moved him away from the danger before she called for help.

qa.q: How might the corn stall owner have felt when Siddharth shouted about the fire?
qa.a: The stall owner probably felt alarmed and rushed to put the lid on the pot and beat out the sheet once Yamini called out.

grounding: Shows a young child freezing and crying at a fire in a crowd, moving away with a grown-up who raises the alarm.

subtype: Learning emergency numbers and who to tell [Actor]
passage: On Friday, Uma ma'am gathered the class in a circle for the safety drill. Each child stood and said a name, a home address and two phone numbers from a card. Ujjwal's knees felt wobbly, but he read in a steady voice: his flat number, the lane, Papa's number and Kaur aunty's number from next door. "And what do you do if your grandmother falls and nobody else is home?" Uma ma'am asked. "Call 112," said Ujjwal. "I say my address and stay on the line. Then I call Kaur aunty." The girl beside him forgot her lane, and Uma ma'am gave her time to try again. Ujjwal put the card back in his bag pocket.

qa.q: Whose number besides Papa's did Ujjwal read from the card?
qa.a: Ujjwal read Kaur aunty's number from next door.

qa.q: What might Ujjwal be feeling as he stands up with wobbly knees?
qa.a: He is nervous but determined, and his steady voice shows the practice is helping.

qa.q: What should the girl beside Ujjwal do to be ready like him?
qa.a: She could practise her address and numbers until she can say them without stopping, using the card for support.

qa.q: How does Uma ma'am help the girl who forgot her lane?
qa.a: Uma ma'am gives her time to try again, so she does not feel judged while she is learning.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild who has practised the emergency number, address and trusted adults, using them steadily when asked.

subtype: Learning emergency numbers and who to tell [Actor]
passage: I live in the flat opposite Gurleen's, so I was in the corridor when Ajji from 4B slipped by the lift, near the wet mop. She sat on the floor, holding her hip, gasping. My mind went blank. Gurleen, who is ten, dropped her school bag, said, "Ajji, we are here," and dialled 112. She gave the building name, floor and flat number without stopping, and said, "She fell. She is awake." Then she told me, "Go and knock on Mehta uncle's door." She looked calm, though I could not tell if she was scared. Later I saw a card in her bag pocket with the numbers written out. Naveen

qa.q: Where did Ajji from 4B slip?
qa.a: Ajji from 4B slipped by the lift, near the wet mop.

qa.q: What might Gurleen be feeling as she dials 112, and what is unclear?
qa.a: Gurleen looks calm and focused, but Naveen cannot tell whether she was scared inside, so her feeling stays uncertain.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do that showed she had practised?
qa.a: She dialled 112, gave the building, floor and flat number, and sent Naveen to knock on Mehta uncle's door.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when Ajji fell?
qa.a: Naveen was frozen and overwhelmed, since Naveen's mind went blank while Gurleen took charge.

grounding: Shows a child who has practised the emergency number, address and who to tell using them calmly, seen by an observer.

passage:
"Someone must have called already," Pankaj said, looking at the scooter lying on its side near the crossing and the rider on the road. About thirty people stood in a ring. Some held up phones.
"Did you call?" asked Sarika.
"No. I thought..."
"Everyone thinks that." She pointed. "You, in the blue shirt, call 112 and tell them the crossing near the bakery. You, with the cap, stop the cars. Pankaj, stay by him and talk. Nobody move him."
Pankaj crouched. "Can you hear me? Help is coming." The man in the blue shirt was already speaking to the operator.

qa.q: Where was the scooter lying?
qa.a: The scooter was lying on its side near the crossing.

qa.q: What is Pankaj feeling when saying that someone must have called already?
qa.a: Pankaj is probably shocked and unsure, and hopes that someone else has taken charge, which lets Pankaj avoid acting.

qa.q: What broke the crowd's waiting, and why did it work?
qa.a: Sarika pointed at specific people and gave each a task, such as calling 112 and stopping cars, so nobody could assume someone else would.

qa.q: How might the rider feel hearing Pankaj say "Help is coming"?
qa.a: The rider might feel frightened but comforted that a person is nearby speaking calmly, instead of a ring of people only watching.

grounding: Shows a teenager in a crowd assuming someone else has called for help until one person names who should call.

passage: I was at the bus stop by the flyover when a man near the shelter dropped to the ground. A crowd formed. I stood at the back, holding my school bag, thinking someone had surely phoned. Phones were up, but I could not see anyone speaking into one. Then Minakshi, who sells tea at the stall, called across, "You with the bag. Call 112. Say the bus stop by the flyover." My hands shook, but I dialled. The operator asked simple questions and told me to stay on the line. Minakshi sat beside the man and kept talking to him. I kept thinking how long I would have stood there. Jagdish

qa.q: Who told the narrator to call 112?
qa.a: Minakshi, who sells tea at the stall, told Jagdish to call 112.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling while standing at the back holding the school bag?
qa.a: Jagdish was probably unsure and frozen, assuming that someone else had surely phoned.

qa.a: Minakshi picked Jagdish out of the crowd and gave a clear instruction to call 112 and say the bus stop by the flyover.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have seen the crowd standing around?

grounding: Shows a teenager in a crowd assuming someone else has called until a person is named to call.

subtype: Basic first aid course and calm hands [Actor]
passage: The power had gone out at the roadside tea stall, and rain hammered the tin roof. Jomon, the cook, sliced through a cloth-wrapped onion in the dark and cut his hand. Blood ran between his fingers onto the wet floor. Rafiq, who had done the college first-aid course in spring, felt his heart race. He made himself check first: the knife was set aside, the floor was slippery, nobody else was near. "Someone call 112," he said, and named a customer. He took a clean cloth and pressed firmly on the cut, holding it there. "Sit down, Jomon, I've got you." He did not lift the cloth to look until help arrived.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq know what to do when Jomon cut his hand?
qa.a: Rafiq had done the college first-aid course in spring.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when he saw the blood, and what did he do with the feeling?
qa.a: Rafiq's heart raced with fear, but he made himself check the scene first and then press on the cut.

qa.q: What would you say Rafiq did well by naming a customer to call 112?
qa.a: Naming one person makes sure the call is made and stops people assuming that someone else has done it.

qa.q: What might Jomon be feeling as Rafiq presses the cloth and says "I've got you"?
qa.a: Jomon is probably shaken and in pain but reassured by a steady person staying with him.

grounding: Shows a trained young adult checking for danger, calling for help and doing only the simple pressure step he was taught.

subtype: Basic first aid course and calm hands [Actor]
passage: In the housing society compound, a boy of nine skidded off his cycle and gashed his knee on the gravel. Sarita, his mother, ran out with her hand over her mouth. Lavanya was passing with her groceries. She had finished a first-aid course last year and her hands were steady, though her chest was tight. First she checked the road was clear and moved the cycle aside. "Sarita, call 112 and give the gate number." Then she pressed a clean cloth on the knee and kept the boy sitting. She spoke calmly, "I am here, it will be all right." When the ambulance came, she told them only what she had done.

qa.q: What had Lavanya finished last year?
qa.a: Lavanya had finished a first-aid course last year.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling and what did she do about it?
qa.a: Lavanya felt tense, with her chest tight, but she kept her hands steady and followed the steps she had learned.

qa.q: What limits of first aid does Lavanya's approach show?
qa.a: She checks for danger, calls for help and only presses on the knee with a clean cloth, leaving anything more to the ambulance team.

qa.q: How might Sarita have felt as she ran out with her hand over her mouth?
qa.a: Sarita was likely scared and panicky, so being given a clear job of calling 112 probably steadied her.

grounding: Shows a trained young adult checking for danger, calling emergency help and using pressure on bleeding, and knowing her limits.

passage: I am Salma, and at twenty I was not trained for anything when a scooter skidded on the bridge road in front of me. The rider lay still. My legs shook. Everyone said, "Lift him, put him in an auto!" I said no. I switched on my hazard lights, put my scooter across the lane, and asked Jahnavi, my classmate who was on the pillion, to wave the traffic back. I called 112 and did what the operator said, one thing at a time. I stayed near the rider and kept telling him help was coming. Not moving him was the hardest part, because everyone wanted to.

qa.q: Where did the scooter skid?
qa.a: The scooter skidded on the bridge road.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling as the rider lay still?
qa.a: Salma was scared, with shaking legs, but chose calm steps instead of panicking.

qa.q: What was the key choice Salma made when others said to lift the rider?
qa.a: Salma refused to lift him, kept the scene safe, called 112 and followed the operator's instructions.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi have felt when asked to wave the traffic back?
qa.a: Jahnavi may have felt nervous but useful, since standing in the road to slow the traffic was a clear task in the middle of a frightening moment.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling an untrained person keeping a scene safe, calling emergency services, staying with the injured and not moving the rider.

passage: The stairwell light was off because of a power cut, and Irawati's phone was at four percent. A thud sounded from the landing below. She found Salma aunty on the floor, holding her ankle, and two neighbours already reaching to pull her up. "Please don't lift her," Irawati said. Her voice shook, but she held her phone torch steady and dialled 112 while the screen still glowed. The operator gave simple instructions, and Irawati repeated them to the neighbours. When the battery died, she borrowed a neighbour's phone to keep the line open. She sat on the step, held Salma aunty's hand and said, "They are on their way."

qa.a: Irawati's phone was at four percent.

qa.q: What is Irawati feeling as she says "Please don't lift her"?

qa.a: Irawati borrowed a neighbour's phone to keep the line open and kept following the operator's instructions.

qa.q: What might Salma aunty need most from the people around her on the landing?
qa.a: Salma aunty probably needs calm company, being told that help is on the way, and not being pulled up while she is hurt.
